question: If AI agents learn to improve themselves, what should people decide must never change?
reflection: Systems that learn from their own mistakes can help us too, if we stay clear about the goals we measure them against.

sources.subject: How AI Agents Are Learning to Rewrite Their Own Stack

one_line: Researchers are turning the parts around an AI model, its instructions, tools and test settings, into things the agent can rewrite and improve on its own.

top_stories.title: Agents that rewrite their own instructions
top_stories.what: Research teams at Microsoft, Google and others describe loops where an agent reviews its past runs, edits its own instruction files or tooling, and keeps only changes that score better on held-out tests.
top_stories.why: Self-improving agents still depend on the measures people choose, so good evaluation design becomes the key human skill.

top_stories.title: A simple rule for where to start
top_stories.what: The overview suggests fixing the narrowest layer first: instructions for repeated procedural errors, tooling for memory or verification failures, and training settings only when the agent stops learning.
top_stories.why: Teams piloting agents for research tasks can use this order to improve results without retraining a model.

idea.title: Evaluation sets for research agents
idea.pitch: Build a small, trusted test set of survey coding and literature tasks in Arabic and English, so any agent a team uses can be checked before and after changes.
idea.first_step: Collect twenty past coding tasks with agreed correct answers to use as a held-out test.

idea_kids.title: Improve the recipe game
idea_kids.pitch: Children follow a simple paper-plane recipe, test how far planes fly, then change one step at a time and keep only changes that help.
idea_kids.first_step: Write a five-step plane recipe card and a simple distance score sheet.
